title: Sky burial
hookLine: in parts of Tibet the body is given to vultures: a last act of generosity, told with respect

lines: A QUESTION AS OLD AS GRIEF.
IN PARTS OF TIBET, THE SKY.
cards: A question as old as grief: when someone we love dies, what do we do with the body? Some bury it. Some give it to fire, some to water.

On the high plateau of Tibet, the ground in places is hard and stony, and wood for a fire is scarce. Over that land, wide-winged and patient, fly vultures. In parts of Tibet, families answer the question with the sky.
This lesson speaks of death, gently, with respect for the families who keep this practice.

teach.h: PRAYERS, THEN A HIGH PLACE AT DAWN.
teach.b: First, what happens, told plainly. After a death, prayers are said and texts read for the one who has died, often for several days. Then, at dawn, the body is carried to a high place set apart for this.

A ritual specialist prepares it, monks or lamas may chant, and the body is offered to the vultures. Families may watch from a distance, or not at all. Tibetans call it jhator, often translated giving to the birds.
Second, why the body can be given. Tibetan teachers say that by this point the mind has left.

teach.h: A HOUSE THE OWNER HAS LEFT.
teach.b: The body is like a house its owner has moved out of: still treated with care, but no longer the person. The person, in this teaching, has gone on into the in-between, the bardo you met in year one. Third, the generosity.

teach.h: THE TIGRESS AND THE GIFT OF A BODY.
teach.b: Giving is one of the perfections a bodhisattva trains in, and Buddhist stories carry it all the way to the body.
In one story of the Buddha's former lives, a young man in the forest finds a tigress so starved she is about to eat her own cubs. He has nothing else to give, so he offers himself.
Sky burial, Tibetans say, carries that same spirit: a body no longer needed becomes food for living beings, so even at the very end something is given. Fourth, the respect owed.

teach.h: A FAMILY'S RITE, NOT A SPECTACLE.
teach.b: This is a family's grief and a sacred rite, not a spectacle.
It leaves a listener far away a quiet question: if the body is a gift, what might we give with it while we are still using it?

how: In parts of Tibet, after days of prayers and readings for the deceased, the body is taken at dawn to a set-apart site, where a ritual specialist prepares it and offers it to vultures while monks may chant; Tibetan teachers describe it as a final act of generosity.

games.why: in the story Buddhists tell of the Buddha's former life, he offers his own body. sky burial, Tibetans say, carries that same spirit of giving.

practice: Go gently: feel your body, your hands, your breath, and think of it as something you've been given for a while; notice what it lets you give today, a hand to help, ears to listen, a voice to say thank you.
If it's hard, rest with the breath, and if a loss feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Sky burial. In parts of Tibet, after prayers and with respect, the body is offered to vultures: a last act of generosity from a body the mind has left. Today's word.
